analysis.one_liner: Toughens federal rules on lead in drinking water, requiring faster notice to residents and full pipe replacement.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate in July 2019 and referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee, where it died without a hearing, a vote, or any action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the federal Lead and Copper Rule, the regulation that governs how much lead is allowed in drinking water. It would require water systems to publicly report every lead test result, notify residents within two days when lead is found above the action level, post online maps of where lead service lines are, ban partial pipe replacement (which can temporarily make lead problems worse), test all taps in schools, and cut the allowable lead level from 15 parts per billion to 10 by 2022 and 5 by 2028.
analysis.who_benefits: Families whose homes are connected to lead service lines — especially households with pregnant women and young children, the groups most harmed by lead exposure — plus residents of cities like Flint and Chicago where lead pipes are common and testing has been spotty. Parents would get plain-language test results for their own taps, and schools would get testing at every drinking water tap.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households with lead water pipes, especially families with children

how_it_helps.text: Water systems must report every lead and copper test result to the EPA or state regulators and make those reports publicly available, including invalidated samples and violation history — closing loopholes where systems could discard bad samples or test favorable sites.

When a test finds lead above the action level, the system must notify the people at that home or building within 2 calendar days and complete an on-site investigation of the lead source within 10 business days.

Water systems must build and publish a public inventory and online map of the material composition and ownership of their service lines within 3 years, so residents can find out whether their own line is lead.

Partial lead service line replacement is prohibited — when a system replaces a line, it must replace it entirely, because partial replacement can shake loose lead particles and briefly raise the lead reaching a home.
The EPA must lower the lead action level to no more than 10 parts per billion by the end of 2022 and 5 parts per billion by the end of 2028, from the 15 parts per billion standard then in effect.

analysis.who_pays: Public water systems, which would bear the cost of more frequent and rigorous testing, service line inventories, full pipe replacement, and faster investigations — costs typically recovered through water rates, so utility customers share part of the burden.

drawbacks.text: Full service line replacement, inventories, and rapid on-site investigations are expensive for water systems, and utilities generally recover those costs through water bills, so ratepayers — including low-income households — would bear part of the cost.

Requiring on-site investigations within 10 business days of every sample above the action level, performed by the water system or local health department, could strain small systems and local health departments that lack staff.
Mandating that every water system test every tap in every school it serves is a large sampling workload, particularly for systems serving many small schools.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health benefit is substantial and one-sided in kind: no level of lead exposure is safe for children, and the main defenses — honest sampling, fast notification, public pipe maps, and full rather than partial replacement — target the exact failures seen in real lead crises. The costs are real but standard for drinking-water compliance, spread across utility budgets and bills over years. The bill is not badly designed; its honest weakness is that it never received the committee scrutiny that would have tested how fast small systems could comply.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in July 2019, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2021, so no hearing, vote, or floor action ever happened.

narrative.text: Sen. Tammy Duckworth introduced the bill on July 11, 2019, joined by Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works the day it was introduced.
The bill attracted one additional cosponsor over its lifetime, a Democrat.
The action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no committee report, and no vote — between referral in July 2019 and the end of the 116th Congress in January 2021.

The bill would have required EPA to rewrite the lead and copper drinking water rule with stricter sampling, public reporting, service line inventories, a ban on partial pipe replacement, and a lower lead action level.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Water utilities benefited from the status quo, keeping the older, looser Lead and Copper Rule that let them report less, sample more favorably, and delay or partially replace lead lines. Residents with lead pipes, who would have gained faster notice and public pipe maps, got none of it from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Water utilities under the old laxer rules

for.name: Sen. Tammy Duckworth
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. John Barrasso (R-WY)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Both named supporters were Democrats and the lone additional cosponsor was a Democrat; no Republican cosponsored and no vote was ever taken, so the bill never showed bipartisan strength.

industries.note: The bill imposes new testing, public reporting, service-line mapping, and full-replacement obligations on water systems, ending practices like discarding unfavorable samples and partial pipe replacement. Utilities generally pass compliance costs to ratepayers, but their interest under the existing rule — lighter reporting and slower replacement — runs against residents' interest in knowing where lead is.

industries.industry: Water pipe replacement contractors and plumbing firms
industries.note: Banning partial replacement and prioritizing high-risk buildings would generate large amounts of full service line replacement work. That work is the same activity that protects residents from lead exposure.
Annual sampling requirements, testing at every school tap, and customer-initiated tests would increase demand for accredited analysis. More testing directly serves residents' ability to detect lead.
